answer: The phrase has been used for different things. The PLO's 1968 charter claimed all of Mandatory Palestine; the PLO recognised Israel in 1993 and voted in 1996 and 1998 to cancel the articles denying it, though Israel disputed that the charter was formally changed. Hamas's 2017 document uses the phrase in a sentence rejecting any alternative to liberating all of Palestine, then treats a 1967-lines state as 'a formula of national consensus' while rejecting the 'Zionist entity'. Likud's 1977 platform claimed the same land for Israel alone. Some who use it today, such as Rep. Rashida Tlaib and 65 Northwestern student groups, say they mean freedom and coexistence. Jewish organisations say it calls for the end of Israel, and in April 2024 the US House called it 'outrightly antisemitic'. Meta's Oversight Board found three posts using it did not break Meta's rules; German courts differ.

facts.text: The PLO later changed its stated position: in a letter to Prime Minister Rabin on 9 September 1993 it recognised Israel's right to exist in peace and security; on 24 April 1996 the Palestinian National Council voted 504 to 54 (14 abstaining) to amend the charter by cancelling the articles contrary to the 1993 letters; and on 14 December 1998, with President Clinton present, council members voted again in Gaza. Whether this formally amended the charter was disputed at the time, including by Israel's government, and we found no published revised text.

could_not_verify: The Likud platform's own Hebrew text and Likud's archive; the English wording comes from the Jewish Virtual Library and is confirmed by a 1977 JTA summary, the Oversight Board and Responsible Statecraft.
The first use of the phrase: sources put it in the mid-1960s PLO or in 1967-69; none gives a dated first use. AJC says its origins are unknown.

A US court or a US university ruling on the slogan: none found readable. The Berlin, Mannheim and Duesseldorf courts and the Meta Oversight Board are cited instead; only Harvard's president is cited from a university, as a statement and not a ruling.
ADL's own page on the slogan could not be loaded; ABC News and the AJC page are used for the Jewish-organisation reading. Hillel's national statements were not read.
The wording of the Berlin court's written reasons: only reports about it (LTO, JNS) were read.

Who translated the English texts. The Avalon pages for the 1968 PLO charter, Middle East Eye's 2017 Hamas document and the Jewish Virtual Library's Likud platform name no translator; none is an official or agreed translation, and readings of single words (for example the date in Article 6 of the charter) are disputed. The Jewish Virtual Library is an advocacy publisher and is labelled so.

A published, revised text of the PLO charter: none was found. The 1996 vote is quoted from Israel's letter to the United Nations (a government source) and the 1998 vote from the Associated Press and the Christian Science Monitor; Arafat's 1998 letter listing the cancelled articles was read only on the Jewish Virtual Library (advocacy) and is not cited. Israel's government held that the charter was never legally amended; the card records the dispute and does not settle it.
not_claimed: This card does not say the slogan is antisemitic, or that it is not. It records what the documents say and what each side says it means.
It does not say that everyone who chants the slogan wants Israel gone, or that none do.
It does not defend Hamas's document, the PLO's 1968 charter, or the Likud platform; it quotes them.
It does not say Likud's 1977 line and Hamas's line are morally the same; it says both claimed the same land for one side.

skeptic.notes: Round three (the last): the only change since round two was the publisher of the Yahoo item. The Yahoo page names the reporter, Marc Rod, but nowhere says Jewish Insider, so I set the publisher to what the page shows (Yahoo News, article by Marc Rod); the quote 377-44-1 is on the page and the origin, yahoo.com, is a different site from Fox, so the fact still has three reliable sources. Nothing else changed. Round two (after the writer's rework). Checked what changed, not the writer's account. New fact 2 (PLO letter to Rabin 9 Sep 1993, PNC vote 504-54-14 on 24 Apr 1996, Gaza vote 14 Dec 1998): each quote is on its page (UN letters, AP via Deseret, CSM, Clinton's remarks); the UN letter from Israel's representative says the pivotal problem is that the resolution 'did not change the covenant', and a PLO official is quoted there as saying the charter is 'frozen, not cancelled', so the card's 'disputed, including by Israel' is accurate and the card says it found no revised text. Reliable sources: UN primary, AP, CSM. Fact 3 now quotes the Hamas sentence together with the next one (the 1967-lines state as 'a formula of national consensus'), so both sides' strongest reading is present. Translator or publisher is named in facts 0, 1, 3 and 4 (none names a translator; the Jewish Virtual Library is advocacy). H.Res. 883: the engrossed text, which I read, carries the same 'outrightly antisemitic' wording as the introduced text cited. Strongest objection now (chanting side): the Tlaib sources are three outlets reporting one tweet, so the 'positive meaning' evidence is two voices; the fact is worded as exactly that and I accept it (nit). Strongest objection (Jewish side): the Oversight Board is labelled primary though its Likud and Hamas lines are its description; each is corroborated by another source (nit). Responsible Statecraft is a think-tank magazine labelled news, consistent with how this repo labels think tanks (nit). No must-fix left.

citer.notes: Round three: no change to the answer or its claims. Round two: the writer rewrote the answer and the fact order shifted, so answer_claims were stale and are redone against the nine facts. Reworded two sentences down to what facts carry: the 1993, 1996 and 1998 sentence now says Israel disputed whether the charter was formally changed (fact 2 says so; the answer did not); 'The Meta Oversight Board found that it has many meanings' is not in any fact (only in contested), so it is replaced by what fact 8 carries, that three posts did not break Meta's rules and German courts differ; 'accepts a state on the 1967 lines' is replaced by the document's own wording. Seven sentences, each tied to facts.
